29.0.0.en: 1 He who shows mercy lends to his neighbor, and he who is generous with his hand keeps the commandments. 2 Lend to your neighbor in the time of his need, and repay what you owe him at its appointed time. 3 Fulfill what you have spoken and be faithful to him; then you will obtain at all times what you desire. 4 Many have counted a loan as a windfall, and have troubled those who helped them. 5 Before he receives, he kisses the hand, and humbles his voice, until he obtains his neighbor's money. 6 But when the time for repayment comes, he delays, and speaks wearisome words, and complains of the turn of the times. 7 If repayment is within his power, he scarcely returns half, and counts what he has returned as a windfall. 8 Otherwise he robs him of his money, and makes him an enemy without cause. 9 He repays him with cursing and abuse, and instead of honor he rewards him with insult. 10 Many have held back because of the wickedness of men, fearing to be robbed without cause. 11 Nevertheless be longsuffering toward the wretched, and do not delay him in giving alms. 12 For the commandment's sake help the poor, and in his need do not send him away empty. 13 Lose your silver for your brother and your friend, and do not let it rust under a stone and be spoiled. 14 Spend your treasure according to the commandments of the Most High; it will profit you more than gold. 15, 16 Shut up almsgiving in your storehouses; it will deliver you from all evil. 17, 18 It will fight for you against your enemy, more than a shield of might and a spear of valor.

29.0.1.en: As Ben Sira speaks of loans that are given to the needy who are in harsh circumstances, he requires both the lender and the borrower to keep the divine commandments. If he who is well-off must support his brother who is in need, then on the other side it befits the borrower not to take advantage of the one who lends to him.

29.0.2.en: He who shows mercy lends to his neighbor, and he who strengthens him by stretching out a helping hand keeps the commandments [1].

29.0.3.en: The true motive for lending is mercy toward the one who is in distress and asks for a loan; by this he keeps the commandments. He gives him the loan and does not ask for interest. He who lends to his needy brother at interest (usury), taking advantage of his need, commits a sin.

29.0.4.en: It befits the believer to distinguish between giving a loan to a person going through a temporary crisis and giving it to a businessman who uses the loan to manage his business, which brings him profit. The first is given the loan without interest. "If thou lend money to any of my people that is poor by thee, thou shalt not be to him as an usurer, neither shalt thou lay upon him usury" (Ex 22:25).

29.1.0.en: Lend to your neighbor in the time of his need, and when you borrow, repay what you owe your neighbor at the appointed time [2].

29.1.1.en: On the part of the lender, it befits him not to be slow if the need is certain; and on the part of the borrower, he must keep faith and repay what he owes of loans without delay [2].

29.1.2.en: v Why then, O rich man, do you desire so late, while you are in hell, what you never hoped for when you were enjoying your luxuries? Are you not the one who ignored the person who was laid at your gate? (Lk 16:20). Are you not the one who despised the poor man (Lazarus), mocking Moses and the prophets? You refused to hold fast to faith in your dealings with your neighbor during his poverty, and now you do not enjoy its pleasant time... This is the way to be in line with the teaching of the Lord: "Make to yourselves friends of the mammon of unrighteousness; that, when ye fail, they may receive you into everlasting habitations" (Lk 16:9). There are poor people here who have no dwelling to receive you in. Make friendship with them by the mammon of unrighteousness, the gains that injustice counts as gains. For there are gains that justice counts as gains; these are found in the treasuries of God. "He that receiveth a prophet in the name of a prophet shall receive a prophet's reward... And whosoever shall give to drink unto one of these little ones a cup of cold water only in the name of a disciple, verily I say unto you, he shall in no wise lose his reward" (Mt 10:41-42), and so by his good things [1].

29.2.0.en: St. Augustine Keep your word, and be trustworthy with him, and you will find what you need in every circumstance [3].

29.2.1.en: It does not befit the borrower to take advantage of the kindness of the lender and be slow or postpone repayment, for he may be in need in the future; and on another side, failure to repay may deprive his needy brethren of finding someone to lend to them.

29.3.0.en: Many count a loan as a sudden, unexpected gain, and bring troubles upon those who help them [4].

29.3.1.en: A man should not hasten to ask for a loan without consideration, for he often brings troubles upon himself and upon others.

29.4.0.en: He kisses the lender's hand until he receives the loan, and to take his neighbor's money he humbles his voice; but when the time of payment comes he postpones, and repays only with words of indifference, and blames the times [5].

29.5.0.en: It is shameful for a man to use a double standard: when he asks to borrow he speaks with humility and gentleness and joy, and exaggerates the promise of repayment on time; but when the appointed time for paying the debt or returning the loan arrives, he turns into another person, and puts off the creditor and tries to evade him, and offers him excuses and reckons that the time is not suitable, and accuses the lender of harshness and lack of mercy. The creditor is then compelled to press him in order to receive even half of the loan, and the two enter into enmity without cause. Sometimes the borrower insults the one who lent to him instead of honoring him. This is what drives some to refrain from giving loans, lest their money be taken from them and they lose friendship [7].

29.5.1.en: When the lender is firm with him, he scarcely recovers half of the loan, and counts that as an unexpected gain; and if the borrower repays nothing, he has robbed him of his money, and counts him his enemy without cause. So the borrower repays the lender with curses and abuse and insult instead of honor [6].

29.5.2.en: Many refuse to lend, not because they are wicked, but for fear of being robbed without cause [7].

29.6.0.en: Nevertheless, be longsuffering with one who is in wretched circumstances, and do not make him wait for your alms [8].

29.6.1.en: Ben Sira calls us to be patient with longsuffering when the one asking for a loan is in harsh circumstances. It befits us to help the poor man and so fulfill his commandment, for it is better than gold and silver [8-11].

29.7.0.en: For the commandment's sake help the poor, and in his need do not send him away empty [9].

29.8.0.en: Lose your money for the sake of your brother and your friend, and do not let it rust under a stone and be spoiled [10].

29.8.1.en: The work of mercy keeps a man's possessions from theft or rust (Mt 6:19-21). And when a man ceases to give, he is like one who keeps his money under a stone, and with the passing of time this money is spoiled.

29.9.0.en: Use your treasure according to the commandments of the Most High, and it will profit you more than gold [11].

29.10.0.en: This expression is a preparation for the saying of the Lord Christ in (Mt 6:19-21) concerning His call: "Lay up for yourselves treasures in heaven." If Ben Sira asks us to keep almsgiving and shut it up in our storehouse [21], that is, in a safe place into which no thief can slip, the Lord Christ came to declare that heaven is our safe place, which all the powers of darkness cannot break into.

29.10.1.en: In the ancient Latin translation (the Vulgate), among some of the Latin Fathers, it reads: "Shut up (store up) your alms in the heart of the poor man." It is as though, when the believer meets a poor man, he sees in his heart a safe treasury in which to deposit his gifts that spring from his loving heart. It is as though the hearts of the believer and of the poor man meet together in Christ Jesus who works in both. He works in the heart of the capable to give with love, and works in the heart of the poor to receive the gift with thanksgiving to the Lord of glory and His generous believers.

29.10.2.en: Shut up almsgiving in your storehouses, and it will deliver you from all sorrow [12].

29.10.3.en: If we wish to preserve what is in our treasury, let us give alms that will keep us in the day of evil. It is a strong weapon for our protection against those who oppose us [12-13].

29.10.4.en: v The good Teacher taught us how it befits us to cleanse the corruption of our body, saying: "Give alms of such things as ye have; and, behold, all things are clean unto you" (Lk 11:41). Do you not see how many remedies there are! Tenderness cleanses us, the word of God cleanses us, as it is written: "Now ye are clean through the word which I have spoken unto you" (Jn 12:9). Not only in this passage, but in other passages as well you have seen the greatness of grace. "Almsgiving delivers from death" (Tob 12:9). "Shut up almsgiving in the heart of the poor man, and it will deliver you in the evil day" (see Sir 29:12) [2].

29.10.5.en: St. Ambrose v We have been baptized and yet we are debtors, not because something was left unforgiven in Baptism, but because we do in our life what we need to be forgiven daily. Those who were baptized and immediately left this world came out of the baptismal font without any sin. But those who were baptized and remained in this life commit uncleanness because of their bodily weakness, which, although it does not cause the ship to sink, needs the help of the pump (to bail it out), or else the water enters little by little and causes the whole ship to sink.

29.10.6.en: Prayer is our calling for help to the pump in keeping the ship from sinking; all voices and hands are used. Now we use our voices when we say "Forgive us our debts, as we forgive our debtors," and we work with our hands when we do this: "To break your bread for the hungry, and to bring the poor who wander into your house" (Isa 58:7). Do a kindness in the heart of the poor man, and he will intercede for you before the Lord (see Sir 29:12) [3].

29.10.7.en: St. Augustine v The remedy for appeasing God has been given to us in the very words of God, for the divine teachings instruct sinners what they ought to do, namely, that God is satisfied with works of righteousness (through the blood of Christ). By mercy they deserve the forgiveness of sin. And it is written in Solomon: "Shut up almsgiving in your storehouses (in the heart of the poor), and it will deliver you from all evil" (see Sir 29:12).

29.10.8.en: And also: "Whoso stoppeth his ears at the cry of the poor, he also shall cry himself, but shall not be heard" (Prov 21:13). For he who shows no mercy cannot be made worthy of the mercies of the Lord. And he who has no humanity toward the requests of the poor gains by his prayers no share of divine compassion. This is what the Holy Spirit declared in the Psalms, affirming: "Blessed is he who regards the poor; the Lord will deliver him in the day of evil" (Ps 41:1).

29.10.9.en: Remember what counsel Daniel gave to Nebuchadnezzar the king when he was troubled and afraid of the grave dream, offering him a remedy to obtain divine help that removes evils, saying to him: "Wherefore, O king, let my counsel be acceptable unto thee, and break off thy sins by righteousness, and thine iniquities by shewing mercy to the poor..." And since the king did not obey him, he fell under the calamities and evils that he saw, which he could have escaped by almsgiving...

29.10.10.en: And the angel Raphael bears witness to the like, urging the giving of alms by choice and with generosity, saying: "Prayer is good with fasting and almsgiving, for almsgiving delivers from death, and purges away sins" (Tob 12:8-9). He shows that our prayers and fasts, unless almsgiving helps them, become less profitable. For he who does them without supporting them by good works has little power in them to reach what he asks [4].

29.10.11.en: St. Cyprian the Martyr It fights for you before your enemy, more than a strong shield and a mighty spear [13].

29.10.12.en: Virtues without almsgiving become barren and fruitless. For the Lord Christ receives the gift of the capable man, and the one who gives alms stores it up for him in heaven, where the enemy of good with all his powers cannot approach it. It is kept for the great day of the Lord, which the wonderful Judge will declare, saying: "I was an hungred, and ye gave me meat..." (Mt 25:35).

29.10.13.en: v Those who will inherit the Kingdom are those who help the poor with good things, and they are sincere Christians who follow the words of the Lord and hope in His promises with confidence. Such is their conduct, for without it their lives, fitting as they are to holiness, would be barren, binding themselves to abstain from sins, so that they do not defile purity, and abstain from drunkenness and theft and the practice of any evil. But if they do not add works of love they remain without fruit, for they keep the first part of the commandments: "Depart from evil," and not the other part, "and do good" (Ps 37:27).

29.10.14.en: So when it is said: "Come, ye blessed, inherit the kingdom" (Mt 25:34), this invitation is not prompted by the fact that they lived in purity, and abstained from theft, nor that they did not exploit the poor, nor seize the possessions of others, nor swear falsely. Rather it is said to them: "For I was an hungred, and ye gave me meat" (Mt 25:35)... They are saved not because they did not sin, but they were saved from their sins by their good works [5].

29.11.0.en: 19 A good man becomes surety for his neighbor, and he who has lost all shame forsakes him. 20 Do not forget the kindness of your surety, for he has given his life for you. 21 The sinner flees from his surety, and the mean-spirited forsakes him. 22 The sinner destroys the goods of his surety, and the ungrateful forsakes his deliverer. 23 There are men who become surety for their neighbor, but he loses all shame and forsakes him. 24 Many were prospering, and suretyship ruined them and tossed them like the waves of the sea. 25 It drove mighty men into exile, and they wandered among foreign nations. 26 The sinner who rushes into suretyship and pursues business dealings falls under judgments. 27 Help your neighbor according to your ability, and take heed to yourself lest you fall.

29.11.1.en: Ben Sira deals with the position of the surety and also of the one who asks for surety [14]. 1. It befits the surety not to be stingy toward his neighbor, so as to refrain from becoming a surety who guarantees him [15-17]. 2. It befits the one whose neighbor has stood surety for him to make every effort to fulfill what is required of him, and not to forsake the one who stood surety for him. 3. A man should not hasten to stand surety for someone who is not trustworthy, nor stand surety for a man beyond his ability. He sums this up by saying: "Help your neighbor according to your ability, and take heed to yourself lest you fall" [20]. In other words, be generous as far as you can, and be prudent for the sake of your peace!

29.11.2.en: The good man stands surety for his neighbor, and he who has lost all shame abandons him [14].

29.11.3.en: The good man acts in the spirit of his Savior, who offered Himself as surety for us while we were sinners, and atoned for our sins and granted us His righteousness. Our Christ became an atoning intercessor for us before the Father although there is nothing good in us. If we refuse to stand surety for our brethren who share our weakness and forsake them, we lose all shame by refusing to be an icon of our Intercessor. A story about suretyship is recorded in The Garden of the Monks:

29.11.4.en: [While a rich young woman was strolling in her garden, she saw a young man trying to commit suicide. She hurried to him and learned from him that he was attempting this because of his many debts and the pressure of the creditors upon him, so he had decided to be rid of life, considering death better than this grievous life. She pledged to pay all his debts even if it cost her all her money. And indeed it cost her most of her wealth. After a little while she became poor and gave herself over to sin. But the merciful God did not will that her labor and love be lost, so He allowed her to fall ill. While she was on her sickbed she came to herself, and repented, and resolved to become a Christian. She asked her neighbors to ask the Pope that she might be baptized, but they doubted her request because of her bad reputation.

29.11.5.en: One night the angel of the Lord stood by her in the form of the man whom she had pitied, and she asked him to help her to be baptized. He reassured her and brought two other angels who carried her to the church, and the three appeared in the likeness of three well-known archons of the city in the king's retinue. When the priests asked them whether they would vouch for her as sponsors, they answered: Yes. So she was baptized and put on the white garments, and the angels returned her to her house.

29.11.6.en: When her neighbors saw her wearing the white baptismal garments they marveled and reported the matter to the Pope, who summoned the priests and inquired of them what had happened. They told him that three of the archons had vouched for her, but when the archons were brought they denied any knowledge of this matter. The Pope then knew that the matter was from God. Then he asked her: What good have you done in your life? She said to him: If I was a sinner and a fornicator, what good could I have done? Then she told him the story of the man for whom she had stood surety. At that she fell asleep in peace, and the Pope cried out, saying: "Righteous art thou, O Lord, and thy judgments are very great" [6].]

29.11.7.en: Do not forget the kindness of the surety toward you, for he gives his life for you [15].

29.11.8.en: As Sirach insists that we support our brethren wisely as far as we can, so on the other side he requires the person not to belittle his surety and forsake him, taking advantage of his love and squandering his money and ignoring the good deed he has done. It befits the one for whom surety was given to be marked by thankfulness and faithfulness, so as to encourage others to continue in doing good and to give surety as far as they can.

29.11.9.en: The sinner squanders the goods of his surety, and the ungrateful man deliberately denies his deliverer [16].

29.11.10.en: Who is the Surety who pays our debts except the Lord Christ? The sinner who does not care for the grace of the Lord and His free work of salvation merely squanders the goods of his Surety.

29.11.11.en: Suretyship has ruined many of the rich, and tossed them like the waves of the sea [17].

29.11.12.en: Suretyship has drawn men of influence and authority from their homes, and they wandered among foreign nations [18].

29.11.13.en: Suretyship has ruined many of the well-to-do who gave their possessions and money as a pledge to rescue those in need, and those they rescued did not care about the position of the surety, who is sometimes compelled to flee from the city.

29.11.14.en: The sinner who risks suretyship and the man who pursues gain fall under judgment [19].

29.11.15.en: The sinner who abuses the love of his surety is occupied with exploiting the surety as much as he can. This sinner, if he escapes punishment in this world, is judged on the day of the Lord.

29.12.0.en: Help your neighbor according to your ability, and take heed to yourself lest you fall [20].

29.12.1.en: Ben Sira advises offering practical love with wisdom, so that suretyship may not cause harm to both parties.

29.12.2.en: v God does not ask you to do good to your neighbor beyond your ability, for thus He says: "Withhold not good from them to whom it is due, when it is in the power of thine hand to do it" (see Prov 3:27; Sir 29:20) [7].

29.12.3.en: St. Barsanuphius v The truth is that if they distribute all they possess to the poor, the members of Christ, in return for one single sin, there is no profit at all, unless they cease from sin and acquire the love that knows no sin (1 Cor 13:4).

29.12.4.en: So let anyone who gives alms in return for his sins begin with Love (Christ) Himself. It befits a person to remember the saying of the Lord: "Thou shalt love thy neighbour as thyself" (Mt 22:39), so that you may realize that it is not fitting for a person to give alms to his neighbor without having pity on himself. Let us also remember the words: "Have pity on yourself your soul and you will please God." How can a person give alms to his neighbor in return for his sins if he does not give alms to himself that pleases God? In the same sense the text gives us the same lesson: "He that is evil to himself, to whom will he be good?" (see 24:5). Surely prayers help in giving alms. Here appears the importance of heeding the words: "My son, hast thou sinned? do so no more, but pray for thy former sins" (see 21:1), that they may be forgiven. The very purpose of almsgiving is that when we pray for the forgiveness of our sins, the prayer is heard. Its aim is not that we continue in our sins, imagining that by alms we pay the price of forgiveness for our sins [8].

29.13.s.en: 3. Be content and do not burden anyone

29.13.0.en: 28 The chief things for life are water, and bread, and clothing, and a house to cover shame. 29 The life of a poor man under a roof of boards is better than sumptuous food in a stranger's house. 30 Be content with little and with much; then you will hear no reproach in the affair of the house. 31 Wretched is the life of a man going from house to house, and wherever he is a guest he does not open his mouth. 32 You feed and give drink to those ungrateful for your kindness, and you are their guest, and after that you hear bitter words.

29.13.1.en: We must not sponge as unwelcome guests, especially by lodging with the rich; for it is better for a man to subsist on what is necessary for life, such as bread and water and clothing and a dwelling that shelters him, and to live in a simple hut, than to sponge on a rich man. By this the believer feels sufficiency and thanks God without murmuring over the deprivation of luxuries.

29.13.2.en: The essentials of life are water and bread and clothing and a house that provides privacy [21].

29.13.3.en: St. John Chrysostom sees that Ben Sira was thinking of righteous Noah, how he lost his dignity and composure even in the eyes of his household because of luxuries and drunkenness with wine.

29.13.4.en: v Noah was the first farmer who tilled the earth and planted a vineyard. He drank of the wine and was drunken, and he lay uncovered in his dwelling.

29.13.5.en: What a dreadful thing! You, beloved, see in drunkenness a dreadful thing, able to dull the senses and put to death the perception of the mind, although Noah was a sensible man to whom the responsibility for all creatures had been entrusted; he was bound with fetters that cannot be loosed, and fell down and became like a lifeless corpse.

29.13.6.en: In truth he became worse than a corpse, for the corpse is unable to do good or evil, but the drunkard is unable to do good, yet becomes more able to do evil; he sprawls and becomes an object of mockery for his wife and children and even the neighbors...

29.13.7.en: What can be more base than a person who is addicted to drink, from whom a foul smell rises to heaven day after day, and who loses his mind? Therefore comes the warning of the wise man: "The life of man is founded on the essentials: water and bread and clothing and a house to cover shame" (see Sir 29:21). So that if anyone falls a victim to drunkenness he does not become a spectacle to the public, and his friends do not look upon him, and he does not become an object of mockery to everyone [9].

29.13.8.en: St. John Chrysostom The life of a poor man under a shelter of logs of wood is better than sumptuous food in the house of a stranger [22].

29.13.9.en: The believer feels secure in the Church, his simple home, more than in enjoying the banquets of the philosophers, which seem sumptuous but are in a foreign land.

29.13.10.en: Be content with little or much, and you will not hear a rebuke that you are a stranger [23].

29.13.11.en: Wretched is the life of the man who moves from house to house, and wherever he stays he dares not open his mouth [24].

29.13.12.en: You entertain guests, and give drink to the ungrateful, and above that you hear bitter words [25].

29.14.0.en: 33 Come, stranger, prepare the table, and if you have something in your hand, feed me. 34 Depart, stranger, from before an honored person; my brother has come to be my guest, and I need the house. 35 Two things the sensible man finds heavy: reproach concerning the house, and the insult of the lender.

29.14.1.en: "Come here, stranger, prepare the table, and if you have something in your hand, feed me [26].

29.14.2.en: Depart, stranger, from before an honored person; there is a more important guest here than you, my brother has come, and I need my house" [27].

29.14.3.en: Two things the wise man finds heavy:

29.14.4.en: Reproach for the household and the insult of the creditor [28].

29.14.5.en: Wisdom is a free gift that the Lord gives to those who fear Him, who keep His commandments, who walk in faith in a spirit of meekness.

29.14.6.en: What occupies the heart of Ben Sira is the fear of the Lord, which gives his heart the spirit of simplicity so that he does not walk with a double heart, that is, limping between two ways, at one time walking in the Lord and at another outside the Lord.

29.15.s.en: Do not leave me in my financial dealings

29.15.0.en: v Your wondrous hand, O my God, lifts my heart above financial dealings!

29.15.1.en: Not to destroy Your financial gifts, but I ask that You not leave me, that I may walk wisely according to Your commandments.

29.15.2.en: In all my dealings be revealed all the more in my depths, and let me fulfill Your will in everything.

29.15.3.en: If my brother asks me for a loan I will give it in Your name.

29.15.4.en: I will neither delay nor hasten, for the sake of the salvation of my soul and the salvation of his soul.

29.15.5.en: I give the loan, and the balance of my love with You increases.

29.15.6.en: If he is able I will ask him for repayment lest greed corrupt him, and I will find the opportunity for another in need.

29.15.7.en: And if I borrow from anyone, let me hasten to repay with sincere thanks from the heart!

29.15.8.en: v If anyone is truly in need I count him the safe treasury of my possessions, which no thief can assail.

29.15.9.en: I count wise giving a weapon for me against the enemy.

29.15.10.en: As I give love and kindness with wisdom and generosity, I hear Your wondrous voice: "I was an hungred, and ye gave me meat."

29.15.11.en: v Grant me to be a wise surety, offering what is within my means.

29.15.12.en: You alone are the Almighty Surety; You stood surety for humanity before Your Father, and paid the price on the Cross!

29.15.13.en: I will not forget Your grace toward me, O divine Surety!

29.15.14.en: I will not deny Your love, for You granted me Your righteousness in place of the corruption that came upon me!

29.15.15.en: Through suretyship You went forth with the Cross to hell; it could not hold You captive, but You destroyed its bonds and released the captives to Paradise!

29.15.16.en: You freed me from the bonds of sin, and You shone upon me, O Sun of Righteousness, so that darkness no longer has a place within me.

29.15.17.en: Let me take shelter in You, and I long for the whole world to enjoy freedom instead of slavery to sin.

29.15.18.en: v You are my treasure and my satisfaction and the rejoicing of my soul; my soul desires nothing but You!

29.15.19.en: If I open my house to one of my brethren, I see You blessing the house and accepting the hospitality.

29.15.20.en: And if someone hosts me, I do not burden him.

29.15.21.en: And at his table I cling to You, who take the last place.

29.15.22.en: As long as I am in this world, wherever I am, I am a stranger and a guest.

29.15.23.en: And as long as my heart moves toward Your heavens, wherever I am, I am at home.

29.15.24.en: Your divine bosom is the place of my rest and my stability.

29.15.25.en: I rejoice in You, for You count me among "the household of God" (Eph 2:19).
